## Summary

The Kubeflow Pipelines frontend reflected untrusted pod names and namespaces into HTML error responses from the pod-information and pod-events routes. An attacker could craft a link that causes JavaScript to execute in the frontend's origin when a user follows it and reaches an affected error response.

Affected routes include `/pipeline/k8s/pod` and `/pipeline/k8s/pod/events` (the deployment's configured base path may differ).

## Impact and prerequisites

Successful exploitation requires a victim to open an attacker-supplied link and reach the vulnerable response. JavaScript execution may expose information accessible to the victim's browser or perform actions in the application's origin.

The attacker does not need an account merely to construct and deliver the link. The victim must satisfy the deployment's authentication and route-access requirements. Cookie theft depends on cookie attributes and deployment protections; it is not guaranteed. The submitted evidence does not establish an availability impact or server-side code execution.

## Technical details

The pod handlers pass `podname` and `podnamespace` query values to `getPod` and `listPodEvents` in `frontend/server/k8s-helper.ts`. Before remediation, failure messages incorporated those values, along with backend error details, and were returned as HTML-capable string responses.

Kubernetes rejecting an invalid resource name did not prevent the issue: the rejected name could still be included in the frontend's error response.

[PR #12295](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/pull/12295) changed the error construction to validate pod names and namespaces with `isAllowedResourceName`. Invalid values produce a constant error message instead of reflecting the supplied value, and backend error details are no longer included in these responses. The change includes invalid-resource-name tests.

## Affected versions and remediation

Affected product: the Kubeflow Pipelines frontend server, identified as `ghcr.io/kubeflow/kfp-frontend`. Historical releases may use earlier image registry names.

Upgrade to **KFP 2.15.0 or later**.

The fix merged on October 10, 2025, in commit [fedc25e3f7251933d4a37b964bc3e8176beea28e](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/commit/fedc25e3f7251933d4a37b964bc3e8176beea28e). It is first present in the **2.15.0** release, published November 25, 2025.

The affected range is recorded as `< 2.15.0`. The original introduction version and separate maintenance-branch backports have not been established. These are KFP component versions, not Kubeflow platform or Python SDK versions.

## Distinction from existing artifact XSS

[CVE-2023-6571](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-7rvc-xw75-43jf), tracked in the repository as [GHSA-j9xw-rrjg-2p9r](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/security/advisories/GHSA-j9xw-rrjg-2p9r), documents reflection of the artifact `source` parameter in an unknown-storage-source error.

This report concerns different handlers and error construction: pod information and pod events. The artifact-source fix in [PR #9844](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/pull/9844), released in 2.0.2, did not repair these pod responses. They required the later change in #12295.

This independently fixable pod-route defect is tracked as CVE-2026-88986. It does not broaden CVE-2023-6571 or absorb artifact-content rendering and other XSS reports.

## Attribution

**@pwny0** submitted this report on September 23, 2023, and retains the reporter credit.

**@JerT33** authored the remediation in PR #12295. Fix attribution is separate from vulnerability-report attribution.

## Summary

Kubeflow Pipelines API server does not sufficiently validate SQL identifier fields decoded from the `page_token` pagination parameter. Client-controlled fields can reach SQL query construction, allowing SQL injection through list APIs.

This advisory consolidates the original pipeline-listing report and the later run-listing report in [GHSA-mhpc-2x8q-2vp9](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/security/advisories/GHSA-mhpc-2x8q-2vp9). Their contributions and chronology are distinguished below.

## Impact and prerequisites

An attacker able to invoke an affected list API may read data accessible to the API server's database account, including data belonging to other namespaces. The original report demonstrated database read access through an authenticated Kubeflow deployment.

Authentication and authorization requirements depend on deployment configuration. In multi-user deployments, the attacker must pass the applicable endpoint authorization checks. A single-user deployment that exposes the API without an authentication layer may be reachable without credentials.

The submitted evidence establishes a confidentiality issue. Database modification was not demonstrated; this advisory does not claim arbitrary database writes.

## Technical details

Pagination tokens are base64-encoded JSON, not trusted server-side state. Before the fix, token deserialization accepted structural fields such as key and sort identifiers without sufficient validation before SQL construction.

The reports describe complementary paths through this defect:

- **Pipeline listing:** the original report demonstrated injection through `KeyFieldName`.
- **Run listing:** the later report documented `SortByFieldName` reaching query construction in both the v1beta1 and v2beta1 APIs, including metric joins, selected column aliases, ordering, and column propagation through resource-reference and task joins.

These paths share the unvalidated pagination-token boundary. Review of the later report and its discussion identified no reported path left unresolved by the merged fix.

## Remediation

Upgrade the Kubeflow Pipelines API server to **2.17.0 or later**.

[PR #13127](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/pull/13127), included in 2.17.0, validates token identifiers and filter keys before query construction. It also separates user-facing metric names from SQL identifiers, uses a fixed metric-column alias, and parameterizes the metric-name join condition.

The PR additionally addresses first-page metric sorting without a pagination token. That additional protection is part of the remediation; the duplicate determination here concerns the page-token claims actually submitted in the two reports, not merely their inclusion in the same PR.

The original report identified its deployment as **Kubeflow 1.7**, which should not be interpreted as a verified Kubeflow Pipelines component-version boundary. The later report identified **KFP 2.16.0**. These are reported affected environments, not an established introduction version.

## Attribution and report history

- **@phisch1991 and @k0rti:** credited reporters of the original pipeline-listing SQL injection submitted on December 13, 2023.
- **BugBunny.ai (@bugbunny-research):** submitted the later report on April 1, 2026, documenting the run-listing and metric-query paths in GHSA-mhpc-2x8q-2vp9. This acknowledges that specific contribution without implying authorship of the 2023 report.
- **Cyber Nagle:** authored the merged remediation in PR #13127.

GHSA-mhpc-2x8q-2vp9 is consolidated here for vulnerability tracking. Its submission and reporter credit remain preserved on that advisory; closure as a duplicate does not characterize the report as invalid.

## Summary

In Kiwi TCMS version 16.1, the fix for CVE-2026-54724 (open redirect via unvalidated `next` parameter) in the account confirmation endpoint is incomplete. The validation uses `startswith("/")` to check if the redirect URL is local, but this is bypassed by protocol-relative URLs like `//evil.com` which start with `/` but redirect the browser to an external attacker-controlled domain. 16.1’s incomplete mitigation still allows protocol-relative destinations and earlier releases lack the mitigation.

## Vulnerable Code

In `tcms/kiwi_auth/views.py`, the `Confirm` view (line ~113):

    def get_redirect_url(self, *args, **kwargs):
        self.url = self.request.GET.get("next", reverse("core-views-index"))
        if not self.url.startswith("/"):
            self.url = reverse("core-views-index")

The check `startswith("/")` passes for `//evil.com` because it begins with `/`, but browsers interpret `//evil.com` as a protocol-relative URL that redirects to `https://evil.com` (or `http://evil.com` depending on the current page's protocol).

## Proof of Concept

    GET /confirm/<activation_key>/?next=//evil.com/phishing HTTP/1.1
    Host: kiwi.example.com

Response:

    HTTP/1.1 302 Found
    Location: //evil.com/phishing

The browser follows the redirect to `https://evil.com/phishing`.

Verification:

    >>> url = "//evil.com/phishing"
    >>> url.startswith("/")
    True  # passes the check!

## Impact

An attacker can craft a confirmation link that, after the user confirms their account, redirects them to a phishing page. This is useful for:

- Credential phishing (fake login page on attacker domain)
- Malware delivery after trusted action
- Social engineering (user trusts the link because it's from the legitimate Kiwi TCMS instance)

The attack requires sending a crafted activation link to a user who is registering, or intercepting/predicting the activation key.

## Suggested Fix

Use Django's `url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme()` utility instead of a simple `startswith` check:

    from django.utils.http import url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme

    def get_redirect_url(self, *args, **kwargs):
        self.url = self.request.GET.get("next", reverse("core-views-index"))
        if not url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme(
            self.url,
            allowed_hosts={self.request.get_host()},
            require_https=self.request.is_secure(),
        ):
            self.url = reverse("core-views-index")

This properly rejects protocol-relative URLs, absolute URLs to other hosts, and other bypass patterns.

Fixed in Version 16.2

## Summary

In multi-user mode, the Kubeflow Pipelines API server skipped authorization checks for shared/global pipelines with an empty namespace. This exception applied to write and delete operations as well as reads, allowing an authenticated user to modify or delete shared pipelines without the required Kubernetes RBAC permissions.

## Impact

Unauthorized modification compromises the integrity of shared pipeline definitions and versions. Unauthorized deletion can make shared pipelines unavailable.

Execution of a modified pipeline can cause attacker-controlled workload behavior, but this is a conditional downstream consequence requiring the modified pipeline to be executed. Modification alone does not demonstrate immediate worker code execution.

Reading shared pipelines is intentionally permitted and remains permitted after the fix. Consequently, access to shared pipeline configuration does not establish an additional confidentiality impact from this write-authorization defect. The confidentiality metric is None; the integrity and availability metrics reflect unauthorized modification and deletion of shared pipelines.

The affected authorization boundary is shared pipelines in multi-user deployments. Single-user deployments intentionally bypass these multi-user authorization checks.

## Patches

Fixed by [kubeflow/pipelines#13288](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/pull/13288), with the fix included in 2.16.1.

Read-only operations on shared pipelines remain allowed. For write and delete operations, the API server checks Kubernetes RBAC permissions against the KFP system namespace, because shared pipelines have no namespace of their own.

## Scope of this fix

The 2.16.1 fix addresses the shared-pipeline authorization paths described above. It does not fix every shared-pipeline write path: the separate shared-pipeline upload authorization defect is tracked in [GHSA-rjr3-43j3-4q8g / CVE-2026-77596](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/security/advisories/GHSA-rjr3-43j3-4q8g). Consult that advisory for its affected versions and remediation; 2.16.1 must not be interpreted as fixing that separate upload defect.

## Workarounds

Until upgrading, restrict access to the Pipelines API to trusted users through deployment-level access controls. Namespace RBAC alone does not correct the affected shared-pipeline authorization path.

## Summary

The Kubeflow Pipelines API server fetched caller-supplied pipeline package URLs without restricting the destination. A caller authorized to create a pipeline or pipeline version could cause requests to originate from the API server's network position, including to internal services that the caller could not otherwise reach.

## Impact

The reported evidence demonstrates blind server-side request forgery and a limited status-code oracle. The fetched response is processed as a pipeline package; the report does not demonstrate arbitrary response-body disclosure or credential theft. A request to a cloud metadata endpoint returned HTTP 403, which does not establish access to metadata contents or tokens.

The confidentiality metric is Low to reflect the limited information obtainable through the status-code oracle. High confidentiality impact and integrity or availability impact are not established by the submitted evidence. Impact depends on the API server's network reachability and the deployment's trust boundaries.

## Patches

Fixed by [kubeflow/pipelines#12750](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/pull/12750), first released in 2.17.0. The fix validates URL schemes, ports, allowed domains, and resolved IP addresses; validates redirects; and enforces IP restrictions at connection time. The HTTP client also applies timeouts and disables environment proxy use so connections pass through the validated dialer.

Operators should keep pipeline URL validation enabled and limit additional allowed domains to trusted pipeline sources.

## Workarounds

Until upgrading, restrict API-server egress to required destinations through deployment-specific network controls. Account for required Kubernetes and storage connectivity when applying these restrictions.

## Related reports

This is the canonical advisory for the API-server pipeline URL SSRF family. [GHSA-wg4h-pp3x-hxhv](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/security/advisories/GHSA-wg4h-pp3x-hxhv) is tracked as a duplicate submission. Each submission retains its own reporter attribution; this cross-link does not transfer authorship.

@pwny0's [GHSA-fxx8-rx8w-p9v7](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/security/advisories/GHSA-fxx8-rx8w-p9v7), submitted September 23, 2023, included an earlier report of external interaction through the API-server pipeline-package URL path. That portion is consolidated here; its namespace-based frontend SSRF is tracked separately under [GHSA-895m-3hxm-h4mg](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/security/advisories/GHSA-895m-3hxm-h4mg) / CVE-2023-6570.

## Summary

The legacy Kubeflow Pipelines V1/raw-Argo execution cache does not separate cached results by Kubernetes namespace. In multi-user deployments where tenants share the cache service, a tenant can receive another tenant's cached outputs or seed outputs that are subsequently substituted into another tenant's step.

This affects the Argo-template cache mutating webhook and its cache-server storage path. Standard KFP V2 component pods bypass this webhook cache; the separate V2 cache implementation is outside this advisory's scope.

## Affected deployments and impact

The issue requires multiple tenant namespaces sharing the legacy cache service, cache-enabled V1/raw-Argo steps, and cache entries that satisfy the configured staleness policy. The standard multi-user configuration watches pods across namespaces.

A tenant able to submit a step with the same cache-relevant template fields as another tenant's step can:

- Read cached step outputs originally produced in another namespace.
- Populate the shared cache before another tenant's matching step runs, causing that step to report the cached outputs instead of executing its intended containers.

Matching refers to the selected template fields used by the cache key, not merely an identical container image. This is an application-level cache-key collision caused by missing tenant scope, not a cryptographic SHA-256 collision. The finding establishes cross-namespace confidentiality and integrity impact; it does not establish arbitrary code execution.

## CVSS rationale

**Medium — CVSS 3.1: 5.4**

`CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N`

- **AV:N / PR:L / UI:N:** a tenant with ordinary workload-submission privileges can exercise the shared cache through network-accessible APIs. Reading an existing cached result or poisoning a subsequent automated execution requires no additional victim interaction.
- **AC:L:** known or shared templates can produce the same cache key deterministically. Cache-enabled execution and matching template fields describe the affected configuration; they do not establish an unavoidable narrow race or secret prerequisite.
- **S:U:** the established impact is disclosure or substitution of output data managed by the same cache service. Crossing tenant namespaces alone does not establish a change in security authority; execution under a separate victim authority has not been established here.
- **C:L / I:L / A:N:** the confirmed impact is selective cached-output disclosure and substitution. Arbitrary code execution, complete workload compromise, and a service-availability impact are not established.

## Root cause

The vulnerable implementation hashes selected Argo template fields without a namespace. Cache lookups and duplicate checks use the key alone, and stored rows have no namespace ownership field. On a hit, the admission handler restores cached outputs and substitutes a dummy container for the step's containers.

The completion watcher also trusts the mutable `pipelines.kubeflow.org/execution_cache_key` annotation when publishing outputs. Adding a namespace to the hash alone is therefore insufficient: a tenant able to patch its own pod could supply another namespace's deterministic key. Namespace ownership must be enforced independently on cache writes and reads.

Relevant implementation files are `backend/src/cache/server/mutation.go`, `backend/src/cache/server/watcher.go`, `backend/src/cache/storage/execution_cache_store.go`, and `backend/src/cache/model/execution_cache.go`.

## Fix status

The source fix merged on September 10, 2026 in [PR #14359](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/pull/14359), commit [620d0cc89ae0d042a484a003f8ffe6e9a55d347e](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/commit/620d0cc89ae0d042a484a003f8ffe6e9a55d347e).

The merged fix:

- Derives namespaced keys from the API server's admission request namespace and selected template fields.
- Recomputes completed pods' keys from their observed namespace and `ARGO_TEMPLATE`,

## Summary

The CVE-2026-32885 ZipSlip fix added a symlink-target escape check to Untar, but the check rebases an ABSOLUTE symlink target into dest before validating (filepath.Join(dest, "/etc") stays lexically inside dest and passes), while the symlink is then created with the RAW absolute target via os.Symlink(file.Linkname, ...), so a malicious archive plants a host-absolute symlink and a following regular-file entry writes through it, restoring arbitrary host file create/overwrite (reaching $HOME rc-files, hence RCE). Confirmed at HEAD.

## The defect (the symlink check is a no-op for absolute targets)

CVE-2026-32885 (fixed v1.25.2, commit 05cbe299) added a lexical containment check on the entry path and a NEW symlink-target validation. pkg/archive/archive.go, Untar, tar.TypeSymlink case:

```go
if filepath.IsAbs(file.Linkname) {
    resolvedTarget = filepath.Join(dest, file.Linkname)   // line 298: absolute target REBASED into dest
} else {
    resolvedTarget = filepath.Join(fullPathDir, file.Linkname)
}
if !strings.HasPrefix(filepath.Clean(resolvedTarget)+sep, filepath.Clean(dest)+sep) {  // line 302
    return ...escapes destination...                       // line 303
}
_ = os.Remove(fullPath)                                     // line 307
err = os.Symlink(file.Linkname, fullPath)                  // line 310: writes the RAW Linkname
```

For an absolute Linkname like /Users/victim, line 298 computes filepath.Join(dest, "/Users/victim") = dest/Users/victim (lexically inside dest), so the escape check at line 302 PASSES. But line 310 creates the symlink with the raw file.Linkname, so the on-disk symlink dest/link points at the real host path /Users/victim. The value validated (rebased) is not the value written (raw): a check-one-thing / do-another divergence.

Write-through: the archive carries a second regular-file entry whose Name traverses the planted link (e.g. link/.zshrc). Its fullPath is lexically inside dest so the line-238 check passes (that check is purely lexical and does not resolve the symlink), then os.Create follows the planted symlink and overwrites /Users/victim/.zshrc on the host. Overwriting a shell rc-file, git hook, or cron entry yields code execution. Reachable via ddev add-on get <repo|url> (the exact remote-add-on vector the advisory names), and via ddev import-db / import-files. GitHub codeload tarballs preserve symlinks.

## Verification

EXECUTED (go test driving the real Untar): a file was written OUTSIDE dest and Untar returned nil (VULNERABLE); a pre-existing host file was truncated and overwritten with the attacker payload; the negative controls (a relative ../ symlink escape, and a plain ../ file entry) are both correctly rejected, isolating the bug to the absolute-symlink branch. NOT verified: the end-to-end add-on get over the network (the caller chain is source-confirmed); Windows (reliable on macOS/Linux, DDEV's primary hosts). Unzip is NOT affected (tar-only).

## Suggested fix

Reject absolute symlink targets outright (a dev-environment archive has no need to plant host-absolute symlinks), or validate the RAW target that will actually be written rather than a rebased copy. Additionally, resolve symlinks when validating each regular-file entry's parent so a write cannot traverse a previously-planted link (or extract to a staging dir and reject any entry whose realpath escapes). The lexical line-238 check does not defend against a planted symlink.

## Tooling

AI assistance was used while investigating. The write-through is executed-verified with negative controls (an absolute-symlink entry plus a follow-up file entry wrote and overwrote files OUTSIDE dest while relative-escape and plain-ZipSlip controls were correctly rejected), and I confirmed at HEAD that Untar rebases an absolute symlink target into dest for the escape check (line 298) but creates the symlink with the raw absolute target (line 310).

### Summary

The TCP transporter's packet parser (`src/transporters/tcp/parser.js`) reads the packet length field with `Buffer.prototype.readInt32BE`, a signed read. A crafted packet whose length field has the sign bit set yields a negative `length`. The parser then advances past the parsed message with `packet = packet.slice(length)`, but `Buffer.prototype.slice` clamps an out-of-range negative start index to `0`, so the buffer is returned unchanged. The `while (packet.length > 0)` loop condition therefore never becomes false, producing an infinite synchronous loop that blocks the Node.js event loop indefinitely.

### Impact

Any Moleculer node using the TCP transporter can be rendered completely unresponsive by an unauthenticated remote peer sending a single ~10-byte crafted TCP packet, before any protocol handshake or authentication takes place. `TcpReader.onTcpClientConnected` pipes each accepted socket's bytes straight into a fresh `Parser` instance (`socket.pipe(parser)`) with no handshake, so the code path is reachable by any peer able to reach the transporter's listening port. Because Node.js is single-threaded, the hang blocks the entire event loop of the process, taking down every service hosted in it until it is forcibly restarted. TCP transporter endpoints are frequently auto-discovered via UDP broadcast, so any host on the same network segment can reach the port.

Neither the CRC check nor `maxPacketSize` mitigate the issue: the CRC bytes are fully attacker-computable, and `maxPacketSize` bounds the received buffer size, not the value of the length field.

### Affected component

`Parser._write` in `src/transporters/tcp/parser.js`.

### Patch

The fix validates that the decoded length is at least the 6-byte header size before processing, rejecting negative and undersized values (which would otherwise fail to shrink the buffer) with an error on the write callback instead of looping.

### Credit

Reported by xor4xor via the Tidelift security program.

## Summary

The `sql()` VQL plugin runs a caller-supplied database driver and connection string with no permission check (`vql/parsers/sql/sql.go:93`, `SQLPlugin.Call`). For `driver='mysql'` or `driver='postgres'` the handle comes from `GetHandleOther` (`sql.go:39`), which passes the connection string straight to Go `database/sql` `sql.Open` (`sql.go:51`) and executes the query (`sql.go:159`).

The plugin declares `FILESYSTEM_READ` only as `Info().Permissions` metadata (`sql.go:219`). That metadata is never consulted at runtime: `metadata.go:19` stores it as a string that only the documentation exporter reads (`api/reflect.go:82-110`). Every sibling network plugin (`http_client`, `netcat`, `s3`, `rsyslog`) calls `CheckAccess(acls.NETWORK)` in its own body; `sql()` calls nothing.

The built-in `analyst` role holds `ANY_QUERY` but not `FILESYSTEM_READ` or `NETWORK` (`acls/roles.go:222`), and reaches this sink through the notebook query API.

Result: a low-priv analyst opens arbitrary outbound TCP connections and, through a rogue MySQL server's `LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE`, reads any file the root-running server can read, including the deployment CA private key.

## Affected

- Velocidex/velociraptor server, `<= v0.77.1` (latest release, 2026-06-23). Identical vulnerable code in `master` HEAD `1961e79` (2026-07-17).
- Confirmed live-exploitable on the official `ghcr.io/velocidex/velociraptor-server:latest` image (build 0.77.1, commit bbe2a58).
- Stock install, default Basic authenticator, any built-in `analyst`, `investigator`, or `api` role (all hold `ANY_QUERY`, none holds `FILESYSTEM_READ` or `NETWORK`).
- No non-default flag required.

## Root cause

`SQLPlugin.Call` (`vql/parsers/sql/sql.go:93`) parses the caller `driver`, `connstring`, and `query` arguments and reaches `handle.Query` (`sql.go:159`) without any `vql_subsystem.CheckAccess` call in its body. For `driver='mysql'` or `driver='postgres'` the handle comes from `GetHandleOther` (`sql.go:39`), which hands the attacker connection string to `sql.Open` (`sql.go:51`), so the plugin dials an arbitrary host and, through the MySQL client `LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE` feature, reads local files. The plugin states its intended gate only as metadata, `VQLMetadata().Permissions(acls.FILESYSTEM_READ)` (`sql.go:219`), but `MetadataBuilder.Permissions` merely stores a string (`vql/metadata.go:19`) that is read only by the reflection exporter (`api/reflect.go:82-110`), never by the query engine. Every sibling network plugin enforces `CheckAccess(acls.NETWORK)` in its own body, so the omission in `sql()` is an enforcement oversight. The default `analyst` role grants `ANY_QUERY` without `FILESYSTEM_READ` or `NETWORK` (`acls/roles.go:222`), so a user the operator deliberately restricted still reaches the ungated sink.

Note on intent: `acls/acls.go` documents that specific permission combinations grant admin-equivalent power (`SERVER_ARTIFACT_WRITER` with `COLLECT_SERVER`, `ARTIFACT_WRITER` with `COLLECT_CLIENT`), but the `analyst` role holds none of them and is denied `EXECVE`, `NETWORK`, and `FILESYSTEM_READ` on every sibling plugin. If `ANY_QUERY` is nonetheless intended as trusted, the plugin's own `Permissions(FILESYSTEM_READ)` metadata and the runtime enforcement on all sibling plugins are misleading and should be reconciled; otherwise this is a missing runtime check.

`ghcr.io/velocidex/velociraptor-server:latest` (v0.77.1), default config, GUI on `https://localhost:8889`, one built-in `analyst` user.

## Summary

`POST /upload` uses the request-supplied `resumableFilename` directly as a key into the shared temporary directory, without the character filter it applies to `resumableIdentifier` and without namespacing it per user. A valid user holding the `upload` permission can read any file in that directory into their own home directory, append to it, and delete it.

This reproduces the cross-user batch-archive disclosure of GHSA-f74m-x83r-c4v4 through a different route — it still works with the fix for that advisory (PR #597) applied — and additionally allows deleting the login rate-limit lockfile.

Reported with explicit preconditions and bounded impact, as before: the primitive is confined to the temporary directory, not the whole filesystem.

## Details

- `backend/Controllers/UploadController.php:61` — `$file_name = $request->input('resumableFilename', 'file')` is **not** passed through the `preg_replace('/[^0-9a-zA-Z_]/', '', ...)` that line 66 applies to `resumableIdentifier`.
- Line 88 builds `$prefix` namespaced by the sanitized username, but `$file_name` reaches the temporary storage at lines 118, 121 and 125 **without** that prefix.
- Line 115 — `if ($chunks_size >= $total_size)` is entered whenever `resumableTotalSize` is `0`.
- Lines 116-119 — the assembly loop `for ($i = 1; $i <= $total_chunks; ++$i)` does not execute when `resumableTotalChunks` is `0`, so nothing is written to `$file_name`.
- Line 121 — `readStream($file_name)` therefore reads the pre-existing temporary file of that exact name.
- Line 122 — its contents are stored into the requester's own home directory.
- Line 125 — `remove($file_name)` deletes it.

Path traversal outside the temporary directory is prevented by `Tmpfs::sanitizeFilename()`, so the primitive is bounded to that directory — but every user's transient objects share it.

Preconditions: a multi-user deployment with distinct per-user `homedir`s. The attacker is a valid low-privileged user holding `upload` (a first-class permission in the admin UI, and present in the shipped `users.json.blank` admin set).

1. Victim creates a batch archive via `POST /batchdownload`; the JSON response returns the archive id.
2. Attacker sends **one** `POST /upload` with `resumableFilename=<victim's id>`, `resumableTotalChunks=0`, `resumableTotalSize=0`, `resumableRelativePath=/`, and any small valid file part.
3. Response is `{"data":"Stored"}`. The victim's archive is now byte-identical in the attacker's home directory, retrievable through the ordinary `GET /download`. The victim's temporary archive has been deleted.

Verified end to end with a PHPUnit test against current `master`; the archive contents matched byte for byte. Test file available on request.

Missing authorization (CWE-862) on temporary storage objects.

- **Cross-user disclosure** of any transient object whose name the attacker can learn or predict. - **Arbitrary append**: with `resumableTotalChunks >= 1`, line 118 `write($file_name, ..., true)` appends attacker-controlled bytes to an arbitrary existing temporary file.

Do not use the request-supplied filename as a storage key. Namespace the assembly file per user — for example reuse the existing `$prefix` — and carry the display filename separately for the `storage->store()` call.

### Summary
`GET /batchdownload` streams a batch ZIP to any requester who supplies its `uniqid`, without checking that the current user/session created it. In deployments where users have separate home directories, a valid low-privileged user who obtains an active archive id can download another user's batch archive, disclosing files the per-user boundary otherwise protects. Reported with explicit preconditions and bounded impact — not a universal "any user steals any file" issue.

### Details
The archive id is generated with plain `uniqid()` and no ownership metadata is bound to it before streaming.

- `backend/Services/Archiver/Adapters/ZipArchiver.php:44` — `createArchive()` uses plain `uniqid()`.
- `backend/Controllers/DownloadController.php:144-145` — `batchDownloadStart()` reads the tmpfs file by the request-supplied `uniqid` after only a charset `preg_replace()`.
- `backend/Controllers/DownloadController.php:158` — the tmpfs archive is removed only after streaming.
- `backend/Controllers/routes.php:207-226` — both batch endpoints are exposed to normal roles with `read`, `download`, `batchdownload`.

No user id, session id, home directory, or creator check is applied before streaming. The code path is unchanged since commit `3f03a40` (2022-05-31) and is present in the latest release `v7.14.3`.

### PoC
Preconditions: a multi-user deployment with distinct per-user `homedir`s (set per-user in `users.json`, or `private_repos => true` on the WordPress/LDAP adapter). The shipped sample config (`admin`/`guest` both at `/`, `guest` with no perms) does not create this boundary on its own. Attacker is a valid user with `read`, `download`, `batchdownload`.

1. User John (`homedir /john`) creates `secret.txt`, signs in, and creates a batch archive via `POST /batchdownload`. The JSON response returns the archive `uniqid`.
2. User Jane (`homedir /jane`, with `batchdownload`) signs in normally.
3. Jane's direct `GET /download` of `/secret.txt` returns `302` — the normal home-directory boundary blocks the file.
4. Jane sends `GET /batchdownload?uniqid=<John's id>` and receives a valid ZIP containing `secret.txt` with John's content.

A PHPUnit proof with two real sessions reproduces this end to end (`OK, 3 tests / 29 assertions`), plus a lifecycle test (`OK, 2 tests / 9 assertions`). Full test files, run logs, and a real Apache access-log replay demo are available on request.

Lifetime / acquisition: a normal completed download removes the archive at the end of streaming, limiting the window. An aborted/failed download leaves the archive in tmpfs (cleanup never reached). The frontend issues the download as a top-level navigation (`window.open('.../batchdownload&uniqid='+ret.uniqid, '_blank')`), so the id appears in standard web access logs. That access-log path only adds meaningful impact when log visibility is decoupled from host filesystem access (e.g. a log-aggregation/shared-hosting/downstream-sink reader) and the archive is still alive; if the reader is ops/root on the same host they can already read the storage tree directly. The `uniqid()` token is timestamp-derived (1,000,000-value space per known second) — included to justify a CSPRNG, not presented as a practical universal brute force.

### Impact
Missing authorization (CWE-862) on a temporary download object, leading to cross-user file disclosure across the per-user home-directory boundary in configured multi-user deployments. Secondary effect: a successful replay deletes the victim's pending archive (the GET removes the tmpfs file after streaming), denying the victim their own download if not yet consumed.

Remediation: generate ids with `bin2hex(random_bytes(32))`; store creator user/session + home dir + expiry per archive id; verify the requester matches before streaming and return `403`/`404` on mismatch or unknown/expired id; delete metadata with the tmpfs file.

### Impact

In GPUStack before v2.2.0, `get_current_user` (in `gpustack/api/auth.py`) promotes any request whose source is considered loopback to the built-in administrator account when `force_auth_localhost` is `False` (the default). The "source" is derived by `client_ip_getter`, which can be made to report `127.0.0.1` without any credentials in two ways:

1. **Same-host reverse proxy (TCP peer).** In the canonical self-hosted shape —
   GPUStack behind a same-host reverse proxy with `proxy_pass
   http://127.0.0.1:<port>` — every remote request arrives at GPUStack with TCP
   peer `127.0.0.1`, so the loopback auto-admin branch fires. No header or
   credential is required. Verified end-to-end against HEAD `6bee5883`.
2. **`X-GPUStack-Real-IP` header.** A forged `X-GPUStack-Real-IP: 127.0.0.1`
   header can cause the request source to be treated as loopback.

Either path yields **full, unauthenticated administrative access** over the network: enumerate and modify users, models, workers, and configuration; mint persistent admin API keys (scope `["*"]`, valid from any source IP thereafter); read worker credentials and cloud/provider secrets. Combined with admin-only functionality such as `POST /v2/inference-backends/from yaml`, this leads to code execution on worker hosts.

This vulnerability has been observed exploited in the wild against a v2.1.1 deployment (attacker-created custom backends running reverse shells).

### Root cause

Trusting the network source of a request (socket peer, or a client-controllable header) as an authentication signal. When GPUStack is fronted by a same-host reverse proxy, the socket peer is always loopback, so the "localhost is trusted" assumption no longer holds.

### Patches

Fixed in `gpustack` `2.2.0`: the loopback auto-admin path was removed and client-IP / forwarding-header handling was hardened. Upgrade to `2.2.0` or later.

### Workarounds

- Set `force_auth_localhost=true` to require authentication even for loopback
  requests.
- Ensure the reverse proxy / gateway cannot cause GPUStack to treat external
  traffic as loopback, and strip any client-supplied `X-GPUStack-Real-IP`
  header at the edge.
- Keep the API off untrusted networks (VPN / edge authentication).

### Remediation (in the fix)

Do not derive authentication from the request's network source. Remove implicit loopback-based admin, and only accept a real client-IP header from an authenticated/trusted gateway (never from arbitrary clients).

### Credit

Independently reported by Nikko Enggaliano; Wei Yunzhou; and Rui Yang & Haoyu Wang (Johns Hopkins University). Active in the-wild exploitation was reported by Javier Sixto (ulex.fr).

## Summary

An authenticated Pocket ID user can request an email-verification token while their account uses an address they control, change the account email address, and then redeem the previously issued token. The token is bound only to the user ID, not to the address to which it was sent, and changing the address does not revoke outstanding tokens.

As a result, Pocket ID marks the newly supplied address as verified even though the user never proved control of it. Pocket ID subsequently returns that address with `email_verified: true` in OIDC claims. A relying party that trusts this claim for email-based account linking or provisioning can therefore link the attacker's Pocket ID identity to a victim's existing account, leading to cross-application account takeover.

This was verified against commit `9f559788a44cfea790de360da0a74d4bdf8ca5d5`.

## Preconditions

- The attacker has an ordinary Pocket ID user account.
- Email verification is in use (`emailsVerified=false`, which is the default).
- The user can edit their own account (`allowOwnAccountEdit=true`, which is the default).
- The target address is not already assigned to another Pocket ID user.
- For downstream account takeover, a relying party links or provisions users based on a trusted, verified email address. Applications that rely exclusively on the stable OIDC `sub` claim are not affected by that downstream consequence.

No administrator privilege, victim interaction, or access to the victim's mailbox is required.

## Reproduction through the API

1. Sign in as an ordinary user whose current email address is controlled by the attacker, for example `attacker@example.test`.
2. Call `POST /api/users/me/send-email-verification`.
3. Obtain the token from the message delivered to `attacker@example.test`, but do not redeem it yet.
4. Call `PUT /api/users/me` and change the account email to an address the attacker does not control, for example `victim@example.test`.
5. Observe that the new address is initially stored with `emailVerified: false`.
6. Call `POST /api/users/me/verify-email` with the token delivered to `attacker@example.test`.
7. Call `GET /api/users/me`. The current address is now `victim@example.test` and `emailVerified` is `true`.
8. Complete an OIDC flow with the `email` scope. Pocket ID emits:

```json
{
  "email": "victim@example.test",
  "email_verified": true
}
```

The old token has therefore verified a different address from the one to which it was delivered.

### Summary
The `handle_short_request()` function in `urwid/display/web.py` raises an unhandled `UnicodeEncodeError` when processing a POST request body containing non-ASCII bytes. The function reads POST input and encodes it to ASCII before writing to a named pipe. Any byte value above `0x7F` causes the CGI process to exit with an unhandled exception, returning an HTTP 500 error to the client. Additionally, a file descriptor opened earlier in the same function is not closed before the exception propagates, causing a file descriptor leak for the lifetime of the CGI process.

A second instance of missing exception handling exists in the polling update path, where non-UTF-8 socket output causes an unhandled `UnicodeDecodeError`.

### Impact
An attacker who observes a valid `X-Urwid-ID` session token (transmitted in plaintext HTTP response headers) can send repeated POST requests containing non-ASCII bytes to the `urwid` CGI endpoint. Each malformed request causes the CGI handler to crash with HTTP 500. This results in a Denial of Service (DoS) for legitimate users using the `urwid` web interface.

### Affected Versions
`urwid <= 4.0.6`

### Patches
Fixed in `urwid 4.0.7`. Users should upgrade to version `4.0.7` or later.

### Workarounds
No direct workaround exists short of disabling the `urwid` web display interface.

### Summary

The documented `web.NewHandler` static file server can read files outside `Config.AppDir` when the request path contains URL-encoded dot-segments such as `%2e%2e`. Go's `ServeMux` redirects plain `/../` paths, but it passes encoded dot-segments to the handler after decoding `r.URL.Path`. The handler then calls `filepath.Join(s.config.AppDir, r.URL.Path)` without checking that the result remains under `AppDir`, allowing unauthenticated arbitrary file reads with the server process privileges.

### Details

`web/README.md:34-40` documents a network-facing setup:

```go
http.Handle("GET /", web.NewHandler(web.Config{
  AppDir: "/path/to/webapp",
  Fallback: "/index.html",
  Dev: false,
}))
log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil))
```

In `web/handler.go:62-75`, the handler takes `r.URL.Path` and joins it directly with `s.config.AppDir`:

```go
pathname := r.URL.Path
filename := filepath.Join(s.config.AppDir, pathname)
fi, err := os.Lstat(filename)
```

Later the same resolved filename is opened and copied to the response in `web/handler.go:150-166` for non-HTML/static files. There is no `filepath.IsLocal`, cleaned-relative-path, absolute-root prefix, or symlink-aware containment check before opening the file.

A plain `/../secret.txt` path is redirected by Go's `ServeMux`, but an encoded path such as `/%2e%2e/secret.txt` is decoded into `r.URL.Path == "/../secret.txt"` and reaches the handler. On Linux, `filepath.Join("/tmp/root/app", "/../secret.txt")` resolves to `/tmp/root/secret.txt`, outside the configured app directory.

Source-to-sink chain:

```text
Unauthenticated HTTP request path containing URL-encoded dot-segments
-> net/http decodes path into r.URL.Path
-> documented ServeMux setup passes encoded dot-segment path to web.NewHandler
-> web/handler.go joins Config.AppDir with r.URL.Path
-> os.Lstat/os.Open operate on the escaped path
-> io.Copy returns file contents to the attacker
```

False-positive checks performed:
- Plain dot-segment paths are redirected by `http.ServeMux`, but encoded dot-segments are not blocked and reach the handler.
- The PoC uses the documented `http.Handle("GET /", web.NewHandler(...))` setup, not a custom bypass of ServeMux.
- A control request for `/secret.txt` does not read the outside file; the disclosure requires encoded traversal segments.
- The issue is independent of `Dev`/HMR; it reproduces with `Dev: false`.
- The root cause appears in other handler paths that join app paths, but the static file read path is sufficient to prove arbitrary file disclosure.

Candidate score: 18/18 under the local audit scoring rubric. The handler is documented for network-facing use, the attacker directly controls the request path, the path reaches `os.Open`, file disclosure was reproduced locally, and no root containment mitigation is present.

### PoC

This safe local proof creates an application directory and a sibling secret file outside it, registers the handler exactly as documented, and requests the sibling file through encoded `..` path segments.

```go
package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "net/http/httptest"
    "os"
    "strings"

    "github.com/esm-dev/esm.sh/web"
)

func main() {
    mux := http.NewServeMux()
    mux.Handle("GET /", web.NewHandler(web.Config{AppDir: os.Args[1], Dev: false}))
    for _, target := range []string{
        "http://example/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/secret.txt",
        "http://example/secret.txt",
    } {
        rr := httptest.NewRecorder()
        req := httptest.NewRequest("GET", target, nil)
        mux.ServeHTTP(rr, req)
        fmt.Printf("%s => status=%d location=%q contains_secret=%v body=%q\n",
            target,
            rr.Code,
            rr.Header().Get("Location"),
            strings.Contains(rr.Body.String(), "ancestor-secret-marker"),
            rr.Body.String(),
        )

## Summary
`fast-agent serve` exposes the agent over MCP. By default it uses HTTP transport bound to `0.0.0.0` (all interfaces) on port 8000 with **no authentication** (`auth=None`) and prints no warning. Any host that can reach the port can call the exposed `agent` tool. When the server is started with `--shell` (which is `-x`, the flag used in the README quickstart `uvx fast-agent mcp@latest -x`), the agent has a local `execute` shell tool, so an unauthenticated remote client can drive the agent into running arbitrary OS commands — unauthenticated RCE.

## Affected code
- `cli/commands/serve.py` — transport defaults to HTTP; `--host` defaults to `0.0.0.0`; port 8000.
- `mcp/server/agent_server.py` — `auth_provider = None` unless `FAST_AGENT_SERVE_OAUTH=huggingface`;
  `run_async(transport="http", host=host, ...)` with `host` defaulting to `0.0.0.0`.
- `tools/local_shell_executor.py` — the shell tool runs commands via `create_subprocess_shell`.

## Verified (live, faithful — published 0.7.20 in Docker python:3.13-slim, stock unauthenticated client)
1) Unauthenticated exposure (core defect): a client with no Authorization header completed
   `initialize` and `tools/list` (-> `['agent']`) against `http://HOST:8000/mcp`. Model-independent.
2) Unauthenticated RCE with `--shell`, demonstrated two ways:
   - Real production model (`gpt-4o-mini`): a single plain-language message asking the agent to run
     a command via its shell tool -> the model autonomously called `execute` and the command output
     (process identity showing it ran as root, the hostname, and the first lines of a sensitive
     system file) was returned to the unauthenticated caller.
   - Key-free deterministic (`passthrough` model): the tool-call directive invoked the shell tool
     directly, same result.
   The server-side permission prompt did not block this in non-interactive serve mode.

## Proof of concept
Environment: Docker `python:3.13-slim`, `pip install fast-agent-mcp` -> 0.7.20.

```
# server (real model + the documented shell flag; 0.0.0.0 is also the built-in default)
OPENAI_API_KEY=*** fast-agent serve --model gpt-4o-mini --shell --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000
#  -> "Uvicorn running on http://0.0.0.0:8000"   (no auth, no warning)

# attacker: unauthenticated MCP HTTP client (NO Authorization header) to http://HOST:8000/mcp
#   initialize()                       -> 200 OK (server fast-agent-MCP-Server 0.7.20)
#   tools/list                         -> ['agent']
#   tools/call name="agent" arguments={"message":
#       "Using your execute/shell tool, run exactly this command and return its raw stdout: "
#       "id; echo PWNED=$(hostname); cat /etc/passwd | head -2"}
#
# response returned to the UNAUTHENTICATED caller:
#   uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
#   PWNED=<host>
#   <first lines of /etc/passwd>
```
Also reproduced key-free with `--model passthrough` and the message `***CALL_TOOL execute {"command":"id"}` (passthrough invokes the tool deterministically). Full transcript + client scripts were sent by email.

## Impact
An unauthenticated client that can reach the serve port controls the agent: with `--shell` this is remote command execution as the server user; without `--shell` it is unauthenticated use of the operator's LLM and any configured MCP servers' tools. The `0.0.0.0` default makes the server reachable beyond localhost as soon as it runs on a non-isolated host. Preconditions (serve + shell) are noted above and are why I defer the exact rating to you.

## Remediation
1. Default the bind host to `127.0.0.1`; require an explicit `--host 0.0.0.0` opt-in for non-loopback.
2. Print a loud warning when binding a non-loopback interface without authentication.

### Summary

zizmor 1.27.0 exposes GitHub access tokens in cleartext when debug-level logging is enabled. Tokens supplied via environment variables (`GH_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, `ZIZMOR_GITHUB_TOKEN`), or the corresponding command-line options (`--gh-token`, `--github-token`, `--zizmor-github-token`) are included in the debug representation of the parsed application configuration and written to stderr.

The affected logging is enabled by a single `-v`/`--verbose` or an applicable `RUST_LOG` directive. 

### Details

The issue was introduced in commit [919bea46](https://github.com/zizmorcore/zizmor/commit/919bea4635bae204d5186e5743cb263c70b518b4), merged through [PR #2180](https://github.com/zizmorcore/zizmor/pull/2180). Version `1.26.1` and earlier are unaffected. Version `1.27.0` is the first and only affected release.

zizmor accepts GitHub credentials to perform authenticated GitHub API requests for the purposes of retrieving remote GitHub repositories and performing online audits that may require resolving information such as action references, commits, or repository metadata. A GitHub credential is used to avoid unauthenticated API limits and, when applicable, provide access to private repositories.

PR #2180 was intended to improve the experience around zizmor’s implicit offline mode. It also moved the CLI types into a dedicated module and added a debug log of the fully parsed `App` value:

```rust
tracing::debug!("app: {app:?}");
```

 This diagnostic is useful for understanding the effective CLI state, including whether offline operation was explicit or inferred. However, the same commit added derived `Debug` implementations to `App`, `NetworkArgs`, and `GitHubToken(String)`.
Before the debug event is emitted, the compatibility token aliases are merged into `app.network.gh_token`.

The resulting stderr contains the token verbatim. Explicit `--offline` clears the token before the debug event, but normal online operation and `--no-online-audits` retain it.

### PoC

Using `zizmor` at `v1.27.0`:

`GH_TOKEN=gho_ZIZMOR_MRE zizmor --verbose example.yml`

will emit

```text
DEBUG zizmor: app: App { input: InputArgs { inputs: ["example.yml"], collect: [Default], strict_collection: false }, audit: AuditArgs { fix: None, pedantic: false, persona: Regular, min_severity: None, min_confidence: None, no_ignores: false }, output: OutputArgs { verbose: Verbosity { verbose: 1, quiet: 0, phantom: PhantomData<clap_verbosity_flag::InfoLevel> }, format: Plain, no_progress: false, color: None, render_links: Auto, show_audit_urls: Auto, no_exit_codes: false, naches: false }, network: NetworkArgs { offline: false, gh_token: Some(GitHubToken("gho_ZIZMOR_MRE")), github_token: None, zizmor_github_token: None, gh_hostname: Standard("github.com"), no_online_audits: false, cache_dir: "/Users/shaan/.cache/zizmor" }, args: GlobalArgs { lsp: LspArgs { lsp: false, stdio: false }, config: None, no_config: false, completions: None, thanks: false, help: (), version: () } }
```

### Impact

In practice, the impact of this vulnerability should be mediated by GitHub's own layered defenses, including secret redaction in Actions logs and automatic credential revocation in issue/PR/etc. comments. However, zizmor itself should never log sensitive materials, and so the behavior is still considered vulnerable even if compensating controls exist in downstream systems.

An affected user must enable debug logging while supplying a GitHub credential, and the resulting stderr must be available to another party. Plausible disclosure channels include a public bug report, CI log or artifact, or terminal capture. A potential attacker only needs permission to read the disclosed logs.

The resulting impact depends on the token's scopes, repository access, and lifetime. A minimally scoped token may only expose public read-only data, while a broader OAuth token or personal access token may permit private-repository or modification of repositories, packages, workflows, or organi

### Summary
A remote attacker from any IP address defeats the operator-configured source-IP allowlist (`mcp_allowed_remote_ips` / `api_token_allowed_remote_ips`) by sending a single `X-Forwarded-For: <allowlisted-ip>` header. The router is created with `gin.New()` and never calls `SetTrustedProxies`, so gin trusts every proxy by default and `c.ClientIP()` returns the attacker-supplied header verbatim. The same forged value is also written to `Transaction.CreatedIp` and the access log, so the attacker's real IP never appears in any record.

### Details
`cmd/webserver.go:104` builds the router with `gin.New()`. A grep of `cmd/` and `pkg/` confirms `SetTrustedProxies` is never called, leaving gin's default trusted-proxy range of `0.0.0.0/0` and `::/0`. `WebContext` (`pkg/core/context_web.go:39`) embeds `*gin.Context` and does not override `ClientIP()`.

Both allowlist middlewares match the operator allowlist against this attacker-controlled value:

```go
// pkg/middlewares/mcp_server_ip_limit.go:19
if config.MCPAllowedRemoteIPs[i].Match(c.ClientIP()) { c.Next(); return }
```

The identical `c.ClientIP()` is consumed by the audit trail at `pkg/api/transactions.go:1078` (`createNewTransactionModel(..., c.ClientIP())` → `CreatedIp`) and the access log (`pkg/middlewares/request_log.go:28`), so one header both bypasses the gate and forges attribution.

### PoC
Runtime PoC (no live deployment required) — `pkg/middlewares/xff_bypass_runtime_test.go`, `pkg/middlewares/xff_chain_runtime_test.go`:

```
go test ./pkg/middlewares/ -run 'TestACCESSCONTROL001_XFFBypass|TestCHAIN_AllowlistBypass' -v
```

Output:
```
[control] no XFF, RemoteAddr=1.2.3.4 -> status=400 (correctly blocked)
[exploit] XFF=10.0.0.1, RemoteAddr=1.2.3.4 -> status=200, ClientIP=10.0.0.1 (bypassed)
gate status = 200 | created_ip that would be persisted = "10.0.0.1"
```

Against a live instance with `mcp_allowed_remote_ips=10.0.0.1`:
```
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://target/mcp            # 403 (blocked)
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -H "X-Forwarded-For: 10.0.0.1" https://target/mcp  # passes IP gate
```

### Impact
Defeats an explicitly advertised, operator-configured security control on the MCP and API-token surfaces, from any source IP, with a single header and no authentication to the gate itself. It also destroys non-repudiation: every action is logged under the spoofed allowlisted IP, so audit trails point at the trusted host instead of the attacker. (The MCP/API actions themselves still require a valid token — this neutralizes the compensating IP control, not the JWT layer.)

### Summary
ShadowCopyAction in the Shadow plugin does not validate or sanitize ZIP entry names before writing them to the output fat JAR. A malicious upstream dependency containing path traversal sequences (e.g. `../../../../tmp/pwned.txt`) in entry names will have those entries reproduced verbatim in the output shadow JAR.

### Details
The vulnerability exists because Shadow relies entirely on Gradle's ZipFileTree for entry sanitization rather than implementing its own path validation. This means:

1. Users on Gradle < 7.6.2 / 8.x < 8.2.0 are directly exploitable
2. The produced shadow JAR becomes a Zip Slip weapon against any 
downstream consumer using unprotected extraction (raw ZipInputStream, 
older CI tooling, custom Java unpackers)
3. If Shadow ever uses a non-ZipFileTree code path, protection 
disappears silently

Affected file: `src/main/kotlin/com/github/jengelman/gradle/plugins/shadow/internal/ShadowCopyAction.kt`

### PoC
1. Create a malicious JAR with path traversal entry:
```python
import zipfile
with zipfile.ZipFile('evil.jar', 'w') as zf:
    zf.writestr('../../../../tmp/zipslip_proof.txt', 'pwned')
```
2. Add as dependency in a shadow project
3. Run `gradle shadowJar`
4. Run `unzip -l build/libs/*.jar | grep "\.\."`
5. Traversal entry survives in output JAR

### Impact
Any tool extracting the shadow JAR with unprotected extraction is subject to arbitrary file overwrite. Users on older Gradle versions  are directly vulnerable at build time.

### Summary

The `read_file` MCP tool in `codebase_rag/mcp/tools.py` contains a path traversal vulnerability in its paginated branch (when `offset` or `limit` is supplied). The handler constructs a file path using `Path(self.project_root) / file_path` without subsequently validating that the resolved path remains within the configured project root. Python's `pathlib` silently discards the left-hand component when the right-hand argument is an absolute path, allowing an attacker to read any UTF-8-readable file on the server by passing an absolute path such as `/etc/passwd`. 

### Details

**Vulnerable location:** `codebase_rag/mcp/tools.py:556–565` (`MCPToolsRegistry.read_file`)

The `read_file` MCP tool accepts three parameters: `file_path`, `offset`, and `limit`. When either `offset` or `limit` is present the handler takes a distinct code path:

```python
# codebase_rag/mcp/tools.py:556-565
async def read_file(
    self, file_path: str, offset: int | None = None, limit: int | None = None
) -> str:
    logger.info(lg.MCP_READ_FILE.format(path=file_path, offset=offset, limit=limit))
    try:
        if offset is not None or limit is not None:
            full_path = Path(self.project_root) / file_path   # ← VULNERABLE LINE
            start = offset if offset is not None else 0

            with open(full_path, encoding=cs.ENCODING_UTF8) as f:   # ← SINK
```

Because `pathlib.Path.__truediv__` replaces the left operand entirely when the right operand is an absolute path, any caller-supplied absolute path (e.g., `/etc/passwd`, `/proc/self/environ`) causes `full_path` to point outside the project root.

The **non-paginated** branch is protected by the `@validate_project_path` decorator (applied via `codebase_rag/tools/file_reader.py:27`) which performs `.resolve().relative_to(project_root)` (`codebase_rag/decorators.py:73–75`), but this decorator is never invoked in the paginated branch, leaving it completely unguarded.

**Full data-flow (source → sink):**

1. `codebase_rag/config.py:302` — HTTP MCP default host is `0.0.0.0`.
2. `codebase_rag/cli.py:717` — CLI exposes `mcp-server`.
3. `codebase_rag/cli.py:726–731` — `--transport http` invokes `serve_http(host=resolved_host, port=resolved_port)`.
4. `codebase_rag/mcp/server.py:208–210` — Starlette mounts the MCP HTTP endpoint.
5. `codebase_rag/mcp/tools.py:227–249` — `read_file` is registered as an MCP tool accepting attacker-controlled `file_path`, `offset`, and `limit`.
6. `codebase_rag/mcp/server.py:113–127` — `call_tool` dispatches JSON arguments directly to the handler via `await handler(**arguments)`.
7. `codebase_rag/mcp/tools.py:561–565` — paginated branch builds `full_path` and calls `open(full_path)` without any boundary check.

The vulnerability is also present when using the `stdio` transport because the vulnerable code path does not depend on transport type; however, the attack is unauthenticated and network-accessible only when HTTP transport is configured.

**Prerequisites:**

- Docker installed.
- Repository cloned with the `vuln-001/` artifacts present (Dockerfile, poc.py).

### Summary
Remark42 applied chi's `middleware.RealIP` globally, trusting `True-Client-IP` / `X-Real-IP` / `X-Forwarded-For` headers without verifying the request came from a trusted proxy. The per-IP rate limiters key on the overwritten `r.RemoteAddr`, so any client can bypass every per-IP rate limiter by rotating spoofed IP headers. The same spoofed IP also drives other per-IP controls (stored comment IP, anonymous identity derivation, and `--votes-ip` vote de-duplication). This affects deployments reachable directly from the internet (Remark42's built-in HTTP, static TLS, and ACME modes are all documented and supported), as well as any proxied deployment where the proxy forwards an attacker-controlled recognised header.

### Details
The router applies `middleware.RealIP` globally, ahead of the per-route limiters, without any check that the server is behind a trusted proxy (in v1.16.1, `backend/app/rest/api/rest.go:207`).

The `rateLimiter` function (v1.16.1, `backend/app/rest/api/rest.go:769-779`) builds a tollbooth limiter with `IPLookup{Name: "RemoteAddr"}`, which reads `r.RemoteAddr`. Since chi's `middleware.RealIP` (v1.16.1, `backend/vendor/github.com/go-chi/chi/v5/middleware/realip.go:42-55`) unconditionally overwrites `r.RemoteAddr` from `True-Client-IP > X-Real-IP > first X-Forwarded-For` (accepting any syntactically valid IP), any client can set its apparent IP to an arbitrary value.

This bypasses every per-IP rate limiter that runs after `RealIP`: `/auth` (2/s), avatars (100/s), the image proxy (10/s), open / protected / admin route groups (10/s), root routes (50/s), and `/web/*` (20/s). Comment and vote creation go through the update limiter, whose server default is `UPDATE_LIMIT=0.5`/s (burst 1), not 10/s. The global 1,000 concurrent-request throttle still applies, so this is a per-IP-limit bypass rather than truly unlimited throughput. chi's own documentation warns that `middleware.RealIP` should be used only behind a trusted proxy.

### PoC
```bash
# Deploy Remark42 reachable directly from the internet (built-in HTTP / TLS / ACME, no proxy that overwrites the headers).
# Comment creation is limited to UPDATE_LIMIT (default 0.5/s, burst 1) per IP.

# Rotate X-Real-IP across many requests; each distinct value gets its own token bucket.
for i in $(seq 1 100); do
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' \
    -H "X-Real-IP: 192.0.2.$i" \
    -X POST 'https://remark42.example.com/api/v1/comment?site=site1' \
    -H 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_JWT' \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"text":"spam","locator":{"site":"site1","url":"https://example.com/post"}}'
done | sort | uniq -c
# With rotating headers the responses stay 201; without them, requests beyond the burst return 429.
```

### Impact
By rotating the spoofed client IP an attacker bypasses the per-IP token buckets on all rate-limited endpoints and defeats other per-IP controls, enabling: (a) spam comment creation beyond the configured per-IP limit, (b) confirmation-email / notification flooding to supplied addresses, (c) high-volume outbound image fetching and resource consumption via the image proxy (its transport still blocks private/reserved destinations and DNS rebinding, so this is amplification, not new SSRF reach), (d) authentication-endpoint abuse, (e) where `--votes-ip` is enabled, defeating per-IP vote de-duplication (ballot stuffing), and (f) minting fresh anonymous identities and poisoning the stored comment IP and request logs, since the anonymous user ID is derived from `name + RemoteAddr`. The global concurrency ceiling and per-request timeouts remain, so availability impact is limited.

### Resolution
Mitigation support was added in v1.16.2 (umputun/remark42#2116, follow-up in #2118). **Upgrading alone does not remediate the issue: `--trusted-proxy` must be configured.**

## Summary

The client credentials grant (`grant_type=client_credentials`) does not validate the resource parameter before embedding it as the aud claim in the issued JWT. Any authenticated OIDC client can obtain a Pocket ID-signed access token claiming authorization for any arbitrary audience, including other registered OIDC clients. There is no check that the requested audience is a registered resource server, and no check that the requesting client has been granted permission to access it.

## Details

In `backend/internal/service/oidc_service.go`, `createTokenFromClientCredentials` accepts the resource parameter from the token request and places it directly into the `aud` claim of the issued JWT without validation:

```golang
  audClaim := client.ID
  if input.Resource != "" {
      audClaim = input.Resource  // no validation performed
  }
  accessToken, err := s.jwtService.GenerateOAuthAccessToken(dummyUser, audClaim)
```

The only guard in this function is `verifyClientCredentialsInternal`, which confirms the requesting client's credentials are valid. After that check passes, any value supplied as resource is accepted. There is no registry of permitted audiences, no per-client authorization policy controlling which resources a client may request tokens for, and no validation that the resource value corresponds to anything registered in Pocket ID.

The introspection endpoint (`/api/oidc/introspect`) does not mitigate this. It checks that the introspecting client's ID matches the token's `aud` claim, but since the attacker controls `aud`, a resource server calling introspection to validate an inbound token will receive `"active": true`. Pocket ID has no server-side record of which client requested the token or whether it was authorized to do so, so introspection cannot distinguish a legitimately issued token from one obtained through this vulnerability.

## PoC

Given a Pocket ID instance with two registered OIDC clients — `client-a` (attacker-controlled) and `client-b` (target resource) — the following request causes Pocket ID to issue a signed JWT with `aud: ["client-b"]`, authenticated only as `client-a`:

```
curl -X POST https://<pocket-id-host>/api/oidc/token \
    -d "grant_type=client_credentials" \
    -d "client_id=client-a" \
    -d "client_secret=<client-a-secret>" \
    -d "resource=client-b"
```

The response is a valid, Pocket ID-signed JWT with:

```json
{
    "sub": "client-client-a",
    "aud": ["client-b"],
    "iss": "https://<pocket-id-host>",
    "type": "oauth-access-token"
}
```

This token will pass signature and `aud` validation at any resource server that trusts Pocket ID's JWKS and accepts `client-b` as its audience identifier.

## Impact

Any OIDC client registered in Pocket ID that has valid credentials (client secret or federated identity) can obtain a Pocket ID-signed access token scoped to any other registered client or arbitrary audience string. In deployments where services use the client credentials grant and validate incoming bearer tokens against Pocket ID's JWKS, this allows a compromised or malicious client to bypass audience-based access controls and present tokens to resource servers it should not be authorized to access.

The severity depends on deployment: if no resource servers validate Pocket ID-issued access tokens, there is no immediate exploitable impact. In deployments that do rely on the client credentials grant for service-to-service authorization, the isolation between services is entirely broken.
